passages.text: But let every door be opened to him, and let all the wretched, enacted laws be dissolved, laws laid down for jealous people. Dominated by folly and unwilling to understand what is reasonable, and also looking suspiciously at the so-called adulterers, these people are reasonably made sport of by Zeus himself through Minos and Rhadamanthys, by means of enacted laws. For Love cannot be restrained once he has taken up residence in souls. The passion of lovers is not voluntary. Indeed, Zeus himself, the lawgiver of these people, had relations with countless women. Some wise men praise him as a benefactor in childbearing, granting human beings union with himself. But among those who, he knew, did not recognize him in connection with the favor, he changed his appearance, so that he would neither distress them nor seem to act against the laws he himself had established. Therefore, for the sake of a good life, you must devote yourself to philosophy and imitate those acknowledged to be superior, whose unions have been countless.

lexical_decisions.chosen: enacted
lexical_decisions.rationale: The laws are instituted or laid down, contrasting humanly established prohibition with the speaker's account of irresistible love. Arbitrary is a possible evaluative reading, but enacted does not add that judgment to the adjective itself.

lexical_decisions.chosen: are reasonably made sport of ... by means of enacted laws
lexical_decisions.rationale: The passive verb describes the jealous people as being played with or mocked, not as themselves playing. The positive judgment reasonably is the letter writer's, and is not silently reversed to match the surrounding narrative's moral position.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: παρ’ οἷς δὲ ἐπὶ τῷ χάριτι ἠπίστατο ἀγνοούμενος
lexical_decisions.chosen: among those who, he knew, did not recognize him in connection with the favor
lexical_decisions.rationale: The passive participle describes Zeus himself as unrecognized or misunderstood, not the favor as unrecognized. The main text takes the former sense while retaining the respect in which he was unrecognized. A material alternative is among those by whom he knew he was misunderstood with respect to the favor; both leave the personal recipients general rather than naming a particular husband or woman.

lexical_decisions.chosen: you must devote yourself to philosophy
lexical_decisions.rationale: The feminine participle addresses the female recipient. The main English does not need a gendered pronoun, but retains the instruction to attend to philosophy rather than treating philosophy as an external agent.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ Ζεὺς αὐτὸς ὁ τούτων, νομοθέτης
lexical_decisions.chosen: Zeus himself, the lawgiver of these people
lexical_decisions.rationale: These is taken as referring to the jealous people just discussed, since the laws are said to have been laid down for them. The lawgiver of these laws is a material alternative, taking the genitive as referring to the previously mentioned enacted laws. The main wording does not claim this referent is grammatically unique.

passages.text: And so as not to waste time needlessly on further proofs, I will begin with Zeus himself, the father of gods and humans, and disclose some of his unions; recalling them all is impossible because of their number. Listen, then, to the unions of great Zeus himself that were concealed through changes of form because of foolish men's jealousy. First, wishing to remove for the wise the supposed sin of adultery arising from different unions, when he was about to marry, and knowing that, as at a first bed, he was not becoming an adulterer according to most people, he obtained a sinless marriage through the supposed sin, as I said. For he marries Hera, his own sister, having made himself resemble the plumage of a cuckoo. From her Hebe and Eileithyia were born. For he gives birth to Metis without union with anyone, just as Hera gives birth to Hephaestus.

lexical_decisions.chosen: different unions
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adjective can indicate differing or varied unions. The context presents the writer's attempt to remove the charge of adultery from multiple unions, but the phrase is not expanded to specify particular partners not named here.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ ὡς ἐπὶ πρώτῃ εὐνῇ κατὰ τοὺς πολλοὺς μοιχὸς εἰδὼς οὐ γινόμενος
lexical_decisions.chosen: and knowing that, as at a first bed, he was not becoming an adulterer according to most people
lexical_decisions.rationale: The unusual first-bed comparison and the appeal to most people's judgment are both preserved. Bed is a sexual or marital union here. The nominative participles are read as Zeus's knowledge of his own not becoming an adulterer; an alternative takes knowing and not becoming as parallel descriptions. The main text does not resolve the argument into an unstated rule about either partner's previous marital status.

lexical_decisions.chosen: having made himself resemble the plumage of a cuckoo
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative literally names a cuckoo's feather or plumage. Plumage preserves that expressed image rather than simply replacing it with the whole bird; a cuckoo's feather is a narrower alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν Μῆτιν γὰρ χωρὶς τῆς πρὸς τινὰ μίξεως ἀποκυΐσκει
lexical_decisions.chosen: For he gives birth to Metis without union with anyone
lexical_decisions.rationale: The active verb assigns the birth to Zeus. The supplied name and unusual parentage are retained rather than harmonized with other versions of the myth.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ τοῦ Διὸς τοῦ πατρὸς θεῶν τε καὶ ἀνθρώπων ἄρξομαι τὰς ἐνίων μηνύειν κοινωνίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: I will begin with Zeus himself, the father of gods and humans, and disclose some of his unions
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive some has an unexpressed referent. The main text follows the immediate focus on Zeus and the next sentence about his hidden unions, treating the selection as unions with some partners. A more source-literal alternative is I will begin with Zeus himself and disclose the unions of some of them, with some potentially referring to the divine beings under discussion. Unions with some partners is another explicit alternative; the English selection of his unions is contextual rather than a claim that the genitive uniquely modifies Zeus.

passages.text: He also has relations with a sister born to him from Uranus and Sea through Cronus's castration, .... Eros and Cypris, whom they also call Didone. He also has relations with Antiope, daughter of Nycteus, having made himself like a satyr; from her Amphion and Zethus were born. He unites with Alcmene, Amphitryon's wife, resembling Amphitryon her husband; from her Heracles was born. He also approaches Aegina, daughter of Asopus, becoming an eagle; from her Aeacus is born. He lies with Amalthea, daughter of Phocus, resembling a bear. He flowed down upon Danae, daughter of Acrisius, as gold; from her Perseus flew forth. For Callisto, daughter of Lycaon, he became a fierce lion, and she bears another, Arcas. He united with Europa, daughter of Phoenix, through a bull; from her Minos, Rhadamanthys, and Sarpedon sprang forth. With Eurymedusa, daughter of Achelous, he became an ant; from her came Myrmidon. With the nymph of Hersaeus he became a vulture; from her came the Palici in Sicily. He united with earth-born Himalia in Rhodes through rain; from her came Spartaeus, Cronius, and Cytus. He took Cassiopeia as a bride, resembling Phoenix her husband; from her Atymnius sprang forth for him. With Nemesis, daughter of Thestius, who was also considered Leda, he became a swan or a goose and fathered Helen; and again, becoming a star, he brought forth Castor and Polydeuces. For Lamia he changed into a hoopoe.

lexical_decisions.chosen: through Cronus's castration
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive can describe a castration associated with Cronus as agent or as the person castrated. Castration carried out by Cronus is a material alternative. The possessive English preserves the association without supplying an otherwise unnamed victim in this clause.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ἔρως καὶ Κύπρις, ἣν καὶ Διδώνην λέγουσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Eros and Cypris, whom they also call Didone
lexical_decisions.rationale: The two names after the printed gap remain a fragment, without an invented verb or genealogical connection. The feminine relative refers to Cypris. Didone transliterates the printed name rather than silently correcting it to Dione.

lexical_decisions.chosen: from her Perseus flew forth
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb's flight image is retained. Sprang forth would be a more idiomatic birth expression but would conceal the explicit flying verb.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Καλλιστοῖ τῇ Λυκάονος ἠγριώθη λέων, καὶ ἄλλον τίκτει Ἀρκάδα
lexical_decisions.chosen: For Callisto, daughter of Lycaon, he became a fierce lion, and she bears another, Arcas
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied lion form and the word another are retained without harmonizing other accounts. The main text infers Callisto as the subject of bears from the childbearing context, assuming an unmarked change of subject. Continuing Zeus as subject is also viable, since τίκτω can describe male begetting: and he begets another, Arcas. The masculine name identifies the child but does not itself determine which parent is the verb's subject.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the nymph of Hersaeus
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive relationship is left broad. Νύμφη can also mean bride or young wife, so bride of Hersaeus is a material alternative. The text is not expanded into a specific genealogy or a different familiar myth.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Νεμέσει τῇ Θεστίου, τῇ καὶ Λήδᾳ νομισθείσῃ, κύκνος ἢ χὴν γενόμενος
lexical_decisions.chosen: With Nemesis, daughter of Thestius, who was also considered Leda, he became a swan or a goose
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both the alternative bird forms and the source's identification of Nemesis with Leda are preserved rather than choosing a single familiar version.

source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints a four-dot gap. The English retains exactly four dots and the following fragment Eros and Cypris, without inventing the lost connection or restoring a missing birth statement. The surviving passage is not represented as an unbroken original.

passages.text: So that I do not spend my time on an endless account, you will find ungrudging unions among all the gods along with Zeus—unions that foolish people call adulteries of the gods. The gods do not even avoid unions with males as shameful, but practice this too as something becoming. Thus Zeus himself loves Ganymede; Poseidon, Pelops; Apollo, Cinyras, Zacynthus, Hyacinthus, Phorbas, Hylas, Admetus, Cyparissus, Amyclas, Troilus, Branchus, Atymnius, Parus, Potnieus, and Orpheus; Dionysus, Adonis, Ampelus, Hymenaeus, Hermaphroditus, and Achilles; Asclepius, Hippolytus; Hephaestus, Peleus; Pan, Daphnis; Hermes, Perseus, Chrysus, Thersus, and Odrysus; and Heracles, Abderus, Dryops, Iocastus, Philoctetes, Ilas, Polyphemus, Haemon, Diomus, and Pirithous.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πάντων μετὰ Διὸς θεῶν ἀφθόνους εὑρήσεις κοινωνίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: ungrudging unions
lexical_decisions.rationale: The source separates this adjective and noun with the verb. The adjective can mean abundant or free from jealousy and grudging; the argument against jealousy supports ungrudging, while abundant unions is a material alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Zeus himself loves Ganymede
lexical_decisions.rationale: The stated erotic love supplies the understood verb for the ensuing series of gods and their named male beloveds. The English preserves every listed person and does not add ages or acts beyond the source.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Hylas
lexical_decisions.rationale: This name in Apollo's list begins with upsilon and a rough breathing. It is distinguished in transliteration from the printed Ἴλα in Heracles' list rather than silently treating the two spellings as identical.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Ilas
lexical_decisions.rationale: The printed iota spelling in Heracles' list is retained as Ilas. Identification with the Hylas in Apollo's list is possible but is not imposed on the source text.

passages.text: Consider for me how many beloved women they rewarded: some they made into constellations, and for some they benefited both children and helpers. Thus Zeus made Callisto into a constellation, the one called the Little Bear, which some also call the Dog's Tail. Poseidon placed Dolphin in heaven because of Amphitrite, and counted Orion, born of Euryale daughter of Minos, worthy of the stars because of Euryale his mother. Dionysus did so with Ariadne's crown. Zeus assigned the eagle that helped in the abduction of Ganymede, and Ganymede himself, a place with the honor of Aquarius; and he honored the bull because of Europa. Moreover, as a favor to Leda, he made Castor, Polydeuces, and Helen into stars; Perseus because of Danae; Arcas because of Callisto; the Maiden, also called Justice, because of Themis; and Heracles because of Alcmene. I will not go on any longer. It would take a long time to detail how many others the gods have benefited because of their many beloved women, through their unions with humans. Foolish people forbid these unions as evil acts, not knowing that pleasure is the great enjoyment among humans.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν λεγομένην ἄρκτον μικράν, ἣν καὶ κυνὸς οὐρὰν προσαγορεύουσίν τινες
lexical_decisions.chosen: the one called the Little Bear, which some also call the Dog's Tail
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both constellation designations and their attribution to Callisto are retained exactly, without harmonizing the passage with a different astronomical identification.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Dionysus did so with Ariadne's crown
lexical_decisions.rationale: The source is an elliptical clause, carrying over the preceding placement among the stars. Did so supplies only that established predicate, not a new celestial act.

lexical_decisions.chosen: assigned ... a place with the honor of Aquarius
lexical_decisions.rationale: Aquarius translates the constellation title Water-Pourer by its conventional English name. The wording attaches the honor to Zeus's assignment; the extent to which the eagle shares the Aquarius description is not resolved by adding a different constellation for it.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the Maiden, also called Justice
lexical_decisions.rationale: The feminine designation is translated as the Maiden, with Justice retaining the meaning of Dike. The source's stray full stop is not treated as a lost-word marker or expanded into an extra gap.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡδονή ἐστιν ἡ μεγάλη ἐν ἀνθρώποις ἀπόλαυσις
lexical_decisions.chosen: pleasure is the great enjoyment among humans
lexical_decisions.rationale: The near repetition of pleasure and enjoyment belongs to the source's maxim. It is retained rather than replaced by a stronger claim that pleasure is the only good or purpose of human life.

source_issues.issue: The selected print places a full stop between the possessive Ganymede and the noun abduction. The English follows their grammatical relationship continuously. This is disclosed editorial punctuation treatment, not a lacuna, restoration, or allegation of OCR error; the supplied Greek remains unchanged.
